papers.summary: This article explores the dynamics of collaborative and participatory innovations in public health services using Chen et al.’s (2020) typology. Based on a mixed survey of projects awarded under the national “Droits des usagers de la santé” initiative, the study finds that user participation primarily generates operational and capacity-oriented innovations frequently involving external partnerships. The analysis highlights the crucial interactions between internal and external dynamics, identifying essential conditions for successful innovations: effective mobilization of internal resources, robust institutional support, and early and active user involvement. However, the study also identifies limitations in citizen engagement, particularly in the evaluation phase of innovations. The article concludes by suggesting avenues for enhancing full co-creation processes in public services to maximize public value.

papers.title: The Decadent Fairy Tale: Queering the Othered Body, 1880-1920

papers.summary: Decadent writers and artists repeatedly drew inspiration from the fairy tale, and reworked the fairy tale into a subversive and experimental adult text. This thesis is the first doctoral study to explore Renée Vivien (Pauline Mary Tarn) and Althea Gyles as writers of decadent fairy tales, and will investigate how Vivien, Gyles, Oscar Wilde, Laurence Housman and Harry Clarke recognized and utilized the potential of the fairy tale to encode subversive representations of the othered body. Such representations have a dual function, in both highlighting the physical alterity present in the fairy tale, and providing a powerful metaphor to communicate experiences of sexual difference. papers.summary: This transdisciplinary, practice-based PhD introduces spectral materialism through art-based research encounters with ecologically and historically stratified land-time-scapes shaped by hypersalinity and colonial terraforming. Centred in the semi-arid Mallee (southeastern Australia) and read through echoes with California’s Imperial Valley, the project examines how spectral time—the co-presence and haunting of other temporalities—manifests in the material conditions of salt, soil, water, plants, and infrastructures. It asks how learning from geological, First Nations, colonial, and ecological pasts can orient responsibilities in unsettled futures. Treating the present as a crisis of time as much as a crisis of matter, the thesis critiques linear-progressive temporalities bound to Western modernity and extractive regimes. papers.title: AI and the Gothic
papers.title_ja: AIとゴシック
papers.summary: For as long as technology has existed, there have been those who are afraid of its implications and wish to roll back its progress. One way in which this has traditionally been effected is through the use of gothic tropes to render new technologies as frightful or vampiric upon either labour or life. In this chapter, I explore the ways that gothic aspects are applied to the new breed of large language models, broadly dubbed AI. Taking a base history of artificial life and its intersection with gothic literatures, such as Frankenstein, but also more contemporary touchstones, this chapter aims to understand how gothic rhetorics influence societal uptake and acceptance or rejection of new technological inventions. This chapter will naturally also explore the unnaturalness of supposedly "playing God" and creating artificial life, a trope very much rooted in gothic traditions.
papers.summary_ja: 技術が存在する限り、その含意を恐れてその進歩を後退させたいと望む人々が存在してきた。本論文は、AIという新しい技術脅威をゴシック的トロープを用いて恐怖的あるいは吸血的として描写する方法を歴史的に検証している。
papers.novelty_reason: AI時代の新しい技術恐怖をゴシック文学の伝統的モチーフで分析することで、古典文学理論と現代的テクノロジー批評を接合した新しい文化批評の枠組みを提示している。
